questions.q: Which condition defines simple harmonic motion?

options.A: The acceleration is proportional to the displacement from equilibrium and directed towards equilibrium.
options.B: The acceleration is constant and directed towards equilibrium.
options.C: The velocity is proportional to the displacement from equilibrium.
options.D: The acceleration is proportional to the displacement and directed away from equilibrium.

questions.solution: In simple harmonic motion the acceleration is proportional to the displacement and always acts towards the equilibrium position: \(a = -\omega^{2}x\). The minus sign shows that acceleration and displacement are in opposite directions.

questions.q: An object oscillates with simple harmonic motion at a frequency of 2.0 Hz. What is the size of its acceleration when its displacement is 0.050 m?
questions.solution: \(\omega = 2\pi f = 2\pi \times 2.0 = 12.6\ \text{rad s}^{-1}\). Then \(a = \omega^{2}x = 12.6^{2} \times 0.050 = 7.9\ \text{m s}^{-2}\). Using the frequency in place of \(\omega\) (0.20) is the usual slip.

questions.q: An object oscillates with simple harmonic motion of amplitude 0.10 m and period 2.0 s. What is its maximum speed?
questions.solution: \(\omega = \frac{2\pi}{T} = \frac{2\pi}{2.0} = 3.14\ \text{rad s}^{-1}\). Maximum speed: \(v_{max} = \omega A = 3.14 \times 0.10 = 0.31\ \text{m s}^{-1}\). It is reached as the object passes through equilibrium.

questions.q: A mass of 0.50 kg hangs from a spring of spring constant \(200\ \text{N m}^{-1}\). What is the period of its vertical oscillations?
questions.solution: \(T = 2\pi\sqrt{\frac{m}{k}} = 2\pi\sqrt{\frac{0.50}{200}} = 2\pi \times 0.050\) = 0.31 s. Putting the fraction upside down (126 s) is the usual slip.

questions.q: What is the period of a simple pendulum of length 1.0 m? (\(g = 9.81\ \text{m s}^{-2}\))
questions.solution: \(T = 2\pi\sqrt{\frac{l}{g}} = 2\pi\sqrt{\frac{1.0}{9.81}}\) = 2.0 s. Forgetting the square root (0.64 s) is the usual slip.

questions.q: The mass of the bob of a simple pendulum is doubled, with the length unchanged. What happens to the period for small oscillations?

options.D: It increases by a factor of four.

questions.solution: \(T = 2\pi\sqrt{\frac{l}{g}}\) contains no mass. A heavier bob needs a larger restoring force, and gets one, because its weight is larger in the same proportion. The period depends only on the length and on \(g\).

questions.q: The mass on a spring is made four times larger. What happens to the period of its oscillations?

options.D: It increases by a factor of four.

questions.solution: \(T = 2\pi\sqrt{\frac{m}{k}}\), so the period is proportional to the square root of the mass. Four times the mass gives twice the period.

questions.q: Where is the kinetic energy of an object in simple harmonic motion greatest?

options.B: Halfway between equilibrium and maximum displacement.

questions.solution: The speed is greatest as the object passes through equilibrium, so the kinetic energy is greatest there and the potential energy is least. At maximum displacement the object is momentarily at rest and all the energy is potential.

questions.q: An object in simple harmonic motion is at its maximum displacement. Which describes its velocity and acceleration at that instant?
questions.solution: At maximum displacement the object stops for an instant before turning back, so its velocity is zero. The acceleration is proportional to displacement, so it is at its largest there, directed back towards equilibrium.

questions.q: An object in simple harmonic motion has amplitude 0.040 m and period 4.0 s. It is released from maximum displacement at \(t = 0\). What is its displacement at \(t = 0.50\ \text{s}\)?
questions.solution: \(x = A\cos\omega t\), with \(\omega t = \frac{2\pi}{4.0} \times 0.50 = \frac{\pi}{4}\) rad. So \(x = 0.040\cos\frac{\pi}{4}\) = 0.028 m. The calculator must be in radians: in degrees it gives almost the full amplitude.

options.A: When the driving force is at its largest.
options.B: When the driving frequency equals the natural frequency of the system.
options.C: When the system is heavily damped.
options.D: When the driving frequency is much higher than the natural frequency.

questions.solution: At resonance the frequency of the driving force matches the natural frequency of the system. Energy is transferred to the system most efficiently, and the amplitude of the oscillations reaches a maximum.

questions.q: The damping on a driven oscillator is increased. What happens to its resonance curve (amplitude against driving frequency)?

options.A: The peak becomes higher and sharper.
options.B: The peak becomes higher and broader.
options.D: The peak becomes lower and broader.

questions.solution: Damping removes energy from the system, so the maximum amplitude is smaller. The peak is also broader, and it moves to a slightly lower frequency. Light damping gives a tall, sharp peak.

questions.q: A system is made to oscillate by a periodic driving force. At what frequency does it oscillate, once it has settled?

options.A: At the frequency of the driving force.
options.C: At the average of the two frequencies.
options.D: At twice the frequency of the driving force.

questions.solution: In a forced oscillation the system is made to vibrate at the frequency of the driving force, whatever its own natural frequency. The natural frequency decides how large the amplitude is, not how fast it vibrates.

questions.q: What happens to a critically damped system after it is displaced and released?

options.A: It oscillates with slowly decreasing amplitude.
options.C: It returns to equilibrium very slowly, without oscillating.
options.D: It returns to equilibrium in the shortest possible time, without oscillating.

questions.solution: Critical damping is the amount of damping that brings a system back to equilibrium fastest with no oscillation. Car suspensions aim for it. More damping than this (overdamping) also stops oscillation, but the return is slower.

questions.q: A pendulum swings in air and is lightly damped. What happens over time?

options.A: Its amplitude and its period both decrease steadily.
options.B: Its amplitude stays the same and its period decreases.
options.C: Its amplitude decreases and its period stays almost the same.
options.D: Its amplitude decreases and its period increases steadily.

questions.solution: Air resistance transfers energy from the pendulum to the surroundings, so the amplitude falls. With light damping the period hardly changes: each swing takes almost the same time, whatever its size.

questions.q: An object oscillates with simple harmonic motion of amplitude 0.020 m and angular frequency \(5.0\ \text{rad s}^{-1}\). What is its maximum acceleration?
questions.solution: The acceleration is largest at maximum displacement: \(a_{max} = \omega^{2}A = 5.0^{2} \times 0.020 = 0.50\ \text{m s}^{-2}\). Forgetting to square \(\omega\) (0.10) is the usual slip.
